name: Treaty with the Potawatomi, August 5, 1836 (Yellow River Treaty)
aka: Treaty of the camp near Yellow River with Pe-pin-a-waw, No-taw-kah and Mac-kah-tah-mo-ah
nations: Potawatomi bands of the Yellow River (Twin Lakes) reserve, Indiana
promises: Article 1: the chiefs ceded the 22 sections reserved by Article 2 of the Tippecanoe treaty of October 26, 1832, which Royce lists as reserved for the bands of Men-o-mi-nee, No-taw-kah, Muck-kah-tah-mo-way and Pee-pin-oh-waw.
Article 2: $14,080 in specie after ratification and on or before May 1 next.
Article 3: the bands would remove within two years to the country west of the Mississippi provided for the Potawatomi nation.
Article 4: a commissioner to pay the band's debts proved just, deducted from the $14,080.
Article 5: the United States would pay the expenses of making the treaty.
today: No court, Indian Claims Commission or government finding about this treaty was found. In 1838, after the two years ran out, the Yellow River band was removed by militia from Menominee's village at Twin Lakes on the march the Potawatomi call the Trail of Death. A Senate resolution introduced on February 13, 2020 (S. Res. 499, 116th Congress) states that Menominee and other leaders refused to take part in negotiating this treaty and later petitioned against its validity; it was referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs, and no record that the Senate adopted it was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's Cultural Heritage Center describes how in September 1838 General John Tipton's militia marched 859 Potawatomi from Menominee's village near Twin Lakes to Kansas with their leaders restrained in a wagon, and more than forty died on what the Potawatomi call the Trail of Death.

openQuestions: The claim that the treaty was signed without Menominee and other headmen of the reserve, and so did not bind them, is the band's long-standing objection; it is stated here only from an introduced Senate resolution and needs a primary source (Menominee's petition to Tipton, the treaty journal, or a court or claims ruling) before it can be weighed. No ruling on the treaty's validity was found.
Whether the $14,080 was paid, and how much went to debts under Article 4, was not traced.

Whether S. Res. 499 (116th Congress) or a later version was adopted was not found; an adopted resolution would be a government statement about the removal but, by its own disclaimer, not about any claim.
The Citizen Potawatomi Nation's account describes the removal, not the treaty terms; it is recorded as the nation's voice, not as a breach.

Whether the Indian Claims Commission or the Court of Claims ever valued the small 1834 to 1837 band reserve cessions in Indiana was not found; the Potawatomi of Indiana and Michigan dockets (29-K and related) and the Commission's 1978 Final Report docket list should be checked.

The Forest County Potawatomi list the 1834 and 1836 band treaties on their treaty pages but give no account of them; which present-day nations descend from this band was not confirmed (treaties.json names the Citizen Potawatomi Nation).
